Metal type is made by inserting a matrix into a hand mould, which is clamped shut and filled with a molten type metal alloy consisting mostly of lead and tin, with a small amount of antimony for hardening; the antimony allows for sharp edges by expanding as it cools. Once the metal has cooled, a rectangular block called a "sort" is extracted. To ensure it is ready for printing, excess casting on the end of the sort, known as the tang, is removed to achieve the precise "type height" required for printing. 

Additionally, letterpunches and counterpunches are produced and hardened to withstand reproduction by striking; counterpunches are hardened through case hardening (exposure to a cyanide solution) or tempering (heating and quenching). Metal types can also be cast from depressions in copper, bronze, iron, or tin created by pressing wooden blocks into sand.
